title: The three states

objectives.can: Tell the absolute, construct and determined states apart and say what each does.

explanation.summary: An Aramaic noun has three shapes, called states. The determined state ends in -ָא and does much of the work of 'the'; the construct state is the short form that leans on the noun after it; the absolute state is the plain form. Reading the state tells you how a noun fits into its phrase.

sections.heading: Three shapes of one noun
body: Besides gender and number, every Aramaic noun carries a state. The corpus labels them Abs (absolute), Cons (construct) and Det (determined, also called the emphatic state). The same noun can appear in all three. Take מֶלֶךְ, 'king': מַלְכָּא is the determined state, and מֶלֶךְ can be the absolute or the construct.

There is no separate word for 'the' in Aramaic and no prefixed article. What marks a noun as definite is the ending of the noun itself. That is the main difference you will notice if you have met a language with a word for 'the'.

sections.heading: The determined state
body: The determined state adds a long ending in -ָא to the noun. In the masculine singular it is -ָא (מַלְכָּא, 'the king'); in the masculine plural it is -ַיָּא (מַלְכַיָּא, 'the kings'). A feminine singular noun takes -ְתָא or -ָתָא (מַלְכוּתָא, 'the kingdom'; מִלְּתָא, 'the word'), and a feminine plural takes -ָתָא (חֵיוָתָא, 'the beasts').

Often this state is best translated 'the'. In Biblical Aramaic the contrast between the determined and the other states mostly holds: a noun in the determined state is normally a particular, known one, and a noun in the absolute state is usually general. It does not hold every time, and in later Aramaic the determined ending weakens until it is just the ordinary form of the noun, so treat 'the' as the usual sense, not an exact rule.
The same ending is also used when someone is addressed: in Daniel 2:37 Daniel says to the king אַנְתְּה מַלְכָּא, which in English is 'you, O king'.

sections.heading: The absolute state
body: The absolute state is the form with no state ending added. It is the form for a noun that is general ('a king', 'kings', 'a word') and for many nouns used as predicates, in lists or with a number. Its plural ending in the masculine is -ִין (מַלְכִין, 'kings'), as in Daniel 2:21, which says that God removes kings and sets up kings.

In Daniel 2:10 the Chaldeans say that no king, however great and mighty, has asked such a thing: מֶלֶךְ רַב וְשַׁלִּיט. Here מֶלֶךְ is the absolute state, and so are the two adjectives that follow it.

sections.heading: The construct state
body: The construct state is the form of a noun that stands directly before another noun and is joined to it in sense: 'king of kings' is מֶלֶךְ מַלְכַיָּא, and 'the word of the king' is מִלַּת מַלְכָּא. The first noun is in the construct state; the second noun, the one that completes it, is in whatever state the sense asks for (here the determined state in מַלְכָּא, so the king is a particular king).

A masculine singular construct often looks exactly like its absolute: מֶלֶךְ is both. A feminine singular construct is usually different, since it ends in -ת where the absolute ends in -ָה or a vowel: compare מִלַּת (construct) with מִלָּה (absolute) for 'word', and מַלְכוּת with מַלְכוּ for 'kingdom'. When a form looks the same, read the next word: if the next noun completes it, it is a construct.
A noun with a pronominal suffix (like אֱלָהָךְ, 'your God') is counted as a construct in the corpus's analysis. Suffixes have a lesson of their own.

sections.heading: Reading the state
body: Look first at the end of the word. -ָא (or -ַיָּא, -ָתָא) points to the determined state. -ִין on a masculine plural, or a bare form, points to the absolute. A noun joined to a following noun, often shortened, is a construct.
In Daniel 2:37 the determined singular, the construct and the determined plural of one noun stand side by side, so that is the first verse below.

misunderstandings: A final א is not always the determined ending. Verb forms can end in א as part of the root or stem: in Daniel 2:21 the participle מְהַשְׁנֵא, 'changing', ends in א but is not a noun in the determined state.
The absolute state is not the same as the English 'a'. Aramaic has no word for 'a'; a noun in the absolute state is simply unmarked, and the translation may supply 'a', 'some' or nothing.
The determined state does not mean 'definite' in every verse. In Biblical Aramaic it usually does, but the ending is already losing its force, so judge by the sentence.
The same spelling can be absolute or construct (מֶלֶךְ is both). The corpus decides by the following word, and so should you.

deeper.heading: Where the ending comes from
body: Grammarians trace the -ָא ending to an old definite marker that was added after the noun, instead of before it as in Hebrew. In the Aramaic of the Bible it still does most of the work of a definite article, but across the history of the language it gradually became the ordinary shape of the noun, until in late dialects the unmarked absolute state almost disappeared from speech. This is why the contrast is firm in Daniel and Ezra yet weaker than a learner of a later dialect may expect.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Thou, O king, king of kings, unto whom the God of heaven hath given the kingdom, the power, and the strength, and the glory;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three forms of one noun side by side. מַלְכָּא is the determined state, 'the king', here used to address him. מֶלֶךְ is the construct state, because it leans on the noun after it. מַלְכַיָּא is the determined plural and completes the phrase: 'king of kings'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said: 'There is not a man upon the earth that can declare the king's matter; forasmuch as no great and powerful king hath asked such a thing of any magician, or enchanter, or Chaldean.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: מִלַּת is the construct of 'word' and מַלְכָּא the determined noun that completes it: 'the king's word'. A few words later מֶלֶךְ, with the adjectives רַב and וְשַׁלִּיט, is the absolute state: 'a great and mighty king'. The English matched to this verse shows the same contrast between 'the king's matter' and 'any king'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: And He changeth the times and the seasons; He removeth kings, and setteth up kings; He giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding;

examples.analysis: The absolute plural in -ִין is מַלְכִין, 'kings', repeated twice. The determined plural -ַיָּא is in עִדָּנַיָּא and וְזִמְנַיָּא, 'the times and the seasons'. חָכְמְתָא is a feminine singular in the determined state.
